opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's honestly one of the things that surprised me most, even as someone who's been thinking about these questions for a very long time. If you'd asked me ten years ago, or even five, I'd have said that to really understand intuitive physics, how liquids flow, how light bounces off surfaces, how materials deform, you'd probably need some kind of embodied experience. You'd need to be a robot acting in the world, or at least an agent in a rich simulation, learning through interaction. That was certainly the view in a lot of neuroscience and cognitive science too.

What Veo shows is that you can get surprisingly far just from passive observation, from watching enormous amounts of video. When you look at the outputs, the way water splashes, the way light reflects off a wet surface, the specular highlights, the way fabric moves, it's not perfect, but it's remarkably good. To generate that coherently frame after frame, the model must have extracted some underlying structure about how the world works. I don't think you can fake that consistently over many frames without some kind of model of the dynamics.

Now, I'd be careful about what kind of understanding this is. It isn't a philosopher's understanding, and it isn't the explicit, equation-based understanding a physicist has. It's more like an intuitive, implicit grasp, closer to how a child understands that a ball will fall or a cup will spill before they could ever write down Newton's laws. In a way, that's the kind of understanding our own brains mostly rely on day to day.

For me this connects to something bigger, which is world models. A system that can model the physics and the causal structure of the world well enough to predict what happens next is exactly what you need for an agent that can plan, imagine, and act, whether that's a robot in your home or a universal assistant that understands the physical context you're in. So Veo isn't only about making beautiful videos, although it does that. It's evidence that these models are learning something real about the structure of reality, and that's one of the key ingredients on the path to AGI.

There's also something philosophically interesting there. If you can learn so much about reality just by observing it, it says something about how much structure there is in the natural world, that it's learnable and compressible. I've long had a hunch that a lot of nature can be efficiently modeled by these kinds of learning systems, and results like this make me more confident in that.

r001.rationale: The response describes Veo’s physics understanding as an intuitive, implicit grasp, but does not identify it as what people sometimes call common sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I find it genuinely fascinating, and in some ways it's one of the more surprising things we've seen come out of these systems. If you'd asked me ten years ago, I would have said that to get a model to understand things like liquids, reflections, how light interacts with a surface, how a ball bounces or a piece of cloth folds, you'd need to explicitly build in some kind of physics engine, some structured prior about the world. And what Veo shows is that you can get a remarkable amount of that just from watching, from passively observing a huge amount of video data. The model has, in some implicit sense, learned a world model. It's picked up on the statistical regularities of how the physical world behaves, and it can extrapolate those in a surprisingly coherent way.

Now, I'm careful about the word "understanding." I think it's an intuitive understanding in the same sense that a young child or an animal has intuitive physics. A cat doesn't know Newton's laws, but it knows how to land on its feet. It has an incredibly good predictive model of its own body and the environment. And I think that's closer to what Veo has. It's not doing symbolic reasoning about forces and masses. It's doing something more like prediction. What should the next frame look like given everything that's come before? And it turns out that to do that well, you have to implicitly capture a lot of the structure of the physical world, because that's what generates the data in the first place.

The part that matters to me, beyond the obvious creative applications, is what it tells us about the path to AGI. One of the big open questions has always been: can you learn a model of the world from observation alone, or do you need to act in the world, to intervene, to run experiments the way a scientist or a child does? And I think the honest answer is that Veo shows observation gets you much further than many of us expected, but it also shows the limits. You still see failures. Objects that pass through each other, things that don't conserve, hands that do strange things. Those failures are informative. They tell you where the model's prior is thin, where it's pattern matching rather than really capturing the underlying causal structure.

So I see it as a stepping stone. If you combine that kind of learned world model with the ability to plan over it, to simulate consequences before you act, that's the kind of architecture that could underpin a much more general agent, something that can operate in the real world, in robotics, or even help us do science by imagining experiments. That was always the dream going back to the earliest days of DeepMind, this idea of a system that builds a model of the world and then uses it to reason. And it's quite something to see pieces of that emerging in a video model, almost as a by-product.

r001.rationale: The response describes Veo as having intuitive physics and an implicit world model, but it does not identify this as what people sometimes call common sense.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s fascinating, because to generate a convincing video, you have to capture something about how the world works. If an object moves behind another object, it should reappear in the right place. If you drop something, it should fall in a plausible way. So the model is learning more than just what things look like—it’s picking up regularities about how they behave over time.

The interesting question is how deep that understanding goes. Has it learned something that generalizes, or is it producing a very convincing approximation that breaks when you put it in an unusual situation? You can’t really settle that just by looking at the best examples. You need to probe it systematically.

But I do think this is an important direction. A model that can predict what happens next in a visual scene has some of the ingredients of a world model. And if you can connect that to actions—what would happen if I did this?—then it starts to become useful for planning, and potentially for robotics as well.

r001.rationale: The response describes Veo learning physical regularities, such as objects falling and reappearing, but does not identify this intuitive physics understanding as common sense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s fascinating, because generating a convincing video requires some understanding of how the world behaves. If a ball bounces, or water flows into a glass, the model has to capture enough of those dynamics for the scene to look plausible over time.

Now, the question is: what kind of understanding is that? I think we have to be careful about equating visual plausibility with a robust understanding of physics. A model might produce something that looks right in a familiar setting, but then fail if you change the conditions in an unusual way.

What I find exciting is the possibility that these models are learning an implicit model of the world just from observing it. To test that properly, you’d want to go beyond generating beautiful videos. Can it predict what happens when you intervene? Can it handle situations it hasn’t seen before? Those are the sorts of tests that would help us distinguish a very good visual approximation from something deeper.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Veo learning world dynamics and an implicit model of the world, but does not identify its intuitive physics understanding as what people call common sense.
